name: ADS7830IPWR
title: ADS7830: 8-bit, 8-channel sampling A/D converter with I2C interface
summary: An 8-bit successive-approximation converter behind an eight-input multiplexer, read and controlled over I2C in standard, fast or high-speed mode, up to 70 kSPS. The inputs work as eight single-ended channels against COM or four differential pairs. It runs from 2.7 V to 5 V, has a 2.5 V reference with a buffer inside that can be switched off for an external one, and powers its converter down between conversions, drawing 180 µW in standard mode at 2.7 V. TSSOP-16, pin compatible with the 12-bit ADS7828, specified from –40 °C to +125 °C.
key_figures: 70 kSPS (3.4 MHz SCL), 10 kSPS (400 kHz), 2.5 kSPS (100 kHz)
180 µW standard, 300 µW fast, 675 µW high-speed mode

circuits.title: Simplified I/O connection
circuits.description: The converter on a 2.7 V to 3.6 V rail beside a microcontroller. The rail feeds VDD through a 5 Ω resistor, with a 1 µF to 10 µF capacitor on each side of that resistor. REFIN/REFOUT has 0.1 µF to ground. SDA and SCL each have a 2 kΩ pull-up to the rail and run to the microcontroller. A0 and A1 are grounded, which sets the bus address to 1001000. The eight inputs and COM are left as inputs from outside.
notes: U2's pins carry the names of the bus lines and supply they connect to.

where.A1, A0: levels on pins 13 and 12, read at power-up

operation.text: A charge-redistribution SAR converter, so sample-and-hold comes with the capacitor array; built on 0.6 µm CMOS. An internal free-running clock drives it. When it is neither converting nor being addressed, the converter core is off and the clock stops.

At the start of hold the selected input is stored on the capacitor array. The source has to charge about 25 pF during sampling; once charged, no more current flows, so the average input current scales with conversion rate.

The internal 2.5 V reference gives a full 0 V to VDD input range on a 2.7 V supply. On 5 V, an external 5 V reference is needed for a full 0 V to VDD range; an external reference may be as low as 50 mV. A smaller reference shrinks the LSB, so offset, gain error and noise look larger in LSBs: noise is about 0.02 LSB peak-to-peak at 2.5 V and about 1 LSB at 50 mV. That noise is Gaussian and averaging successive results reduces it.

The part is a slave on SDA and SCL, both open drain, in standard (100 kHz), fast (400 kHz) and high-speed (3.4 MHz) modes. It acts as slave receiver when written and slave transmitter when read. Each byte is acknowledged on a ninth clock; the master ends a read by not acknowledging the last byte.

The top five address bits are fixed at 10010. A1 and A0, tied to VDD or digital ground and sampled at power-up, give the next two, so up to four converters share a bus. The part acknowledges once it sees its address and the R/W bit.

After a write-address, the converter powers up and begins converting on receipt of bit 4 of the command byte, then acknowledges a valid command. Data can be read only after a conversion has been started this way.

operation.topic: Reading in standard and fast mode
operation.text: Write-address, command byte, then a repeated START, read-address, and one data byte D7 to D0 which the master answers with not-acknowledge and STOP. Ending with a repeated START instead keeps the bus and loops back to the write-address for the next conversion, the quickest way to convert continuously. After the read the converter goes to the state the power-down bits set.

The master sends the HS master code 00001XXX in F/S mode, then the same write and read sequence follows at high speed. A conversion cannot finish between the repeated START and the read-address, so the part holds SCL low after the read-address byte until the result is ready. A STOP returns the bus to F/S mode; a repeated START keeps it in HS mode.

The internal reference is off at power-up. To use it, every command byte must carry PD1 = 1. It turns on only once a command with PD1 = 1 is followed by a STOP or repeated START; later commands with PD1 = 1 just keep it on, and any command with PD1 = 0 turns it off. Each time it comes back on, allow it to settle to 8-bit accuracy before converting (37 µs with no capacitor, 930 µs with 1 µF). A recommended sequence is a write of a command with PD1 = 1 and a STOP, a wait for settling, and then the normal read sequence. With an external reference, PD1 is 0 and the reference must be settled first.

A SAR conversion has one decision window per bit in which a glitch on supply, reference, ground or digital inputs corrupts the result; switching supplies, digital logic and high-power parts are typical sources. Place a 0.1 µF ceramic bypass as close to the part as possible, and add 1 µF to 10 µF when the connection from the supply to +VDD has high impedance. An external reference has no rejection of its own: tied to the supply, the supply's noise and ripple go straight into the codes, and 50 Hz or 60 Hz variation is hard to filter. Return GND to a clean, analog ground point away from a microcontroller's or DSP's ground, ideally an analog ground plane for the converter and its analog circuits.
